title: A Teaching Poem on Diabetes
intro: Husam al-Dosari, a specialist in childhood diabetes, fits names such as LADA and MODY into Arabic couplets whose two halves rhyme anew each time. He takes us from a doctor puzzled over a diagnosis to Leonard Thompson’s bedside in Toronto in 1922, and finally makes room for the patient and family at the head of the care team. The poem gives the boy a single moment of apparent recovery. His hospital chart records two treatments twelve days apart, and the University of Toronto’s exhibition tells us that he lived another thirteen years on insulin.

translation: In the name of the Merciful, who raised the sky
and sent down healing and remedies.
1.sharh: The opening looks upwards at the sky and then downwards towards the sick. Naming healing and its remedies together leaves a place in the prayer for the human work of finding a medicine.

translation: I praise Him for His great bounty,
His kindness to us in our condition and His justice.
2.sharh: Broad divine generosity is brought down to “our condition”. The physician includes himself among those who need the kindness for which he gives thanks.

translation: Then blessings, and after them peace,
upon the Prophet for as long as a cloud rises.
3.sharh: The customary blessing is given a measure of time that a listener can picture. Every cloud that rises offers another occasion for it.

translation: Here is a poem in rajaz that I have composed.
I did all I could in gathering it together.
4.sharh: Rajaz has a long history as a teaching metre. Here each couplet finds its own rhyme, giving unfamiliar medical terms a fresh pair of lines in which to settle.

translation: I have written about a disease that spread far and wide.
Its name travelled, rose and filled the air.
5.sharh: The disease spreads first among people and then through what people say. The poet makes his listener hear that spreading reputation before he supplies the name.

translation: They called it diabetes. They said
there were many different ways to describe it.
6.sharh: One familiar name covers a number of conditions with different causes. The speaker hands the floor to the physicians whose distinctions he is about to put into verse.

translation: Its varieties are numerous and diverse.
They did well to sum them up under four headings.
7.sharh: Four headings make a convenient teaching scheme. A widely used clinical classification groups type 1, type 2, gestational diabetes and other specific forms, the last of which contains many distinct conditions.

translation: The best known in my time
are two widespread kinds, the first and the second.
8.sharh: He starts with the two names his audience is most likely to recognise. The numbers name types of diabetes and carry no implication that a person passes from one stage to the next.

translation: The first picked out children for itself
and took its toll on their endocrine gland.
9.sharh: Type 1 is cast as a visitor choosing children. Its common autoimmune form destroys insulin-producing cells in the pancreas and can first appear at any age.

translation: But when it hides and takes another course,
among adults it takes the name LADA.
10.sharh: LADA is a term for slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes first recognised in an adult. The hidden traveller captures that gradual onset, though adult-onset type 1 can also develop rapidly.

translation: The second kind keeps growing.
It has roamed through the world without a bridle.
11.sharh: The spreading disease takes on the form of a horse roaming unchecked. What grows here is the reach of type 2 diabetes across populations.

translation: The third kind visits the pregnant woman
and departs when they cut the cord.
12.sharh: The cut cord gives birth a single visible instant. Blood glucose often falls after delivery, but cutting the cord is no treatment and a postpartum test establishes whether high glucose persists.

translation: Yet sometimes it settles in and will not relent.
Sometimes it comes visiting after deserting her.
13.sharh: The visitor may stay or make another appearance years later. People who have had gestational diabetes have a higher future risk of type 2, giving follow-up a purpose long after pregnancy.

translation: On the fourth heading they spoke at length.
They kept enumerating its forms and went on and on.
14.sharh: The fourth heading gathers conditions of quite different origins, including some caused by a change in a single gene. The paired verbs let the listener feel how long the full list could become.

translation: By way of example, without exhausting the list,
take the young person’s form. Say “MODY”.
15.sharh: MODY stands for maturity-onset diabetes of the young. It covers several single-gene forms, often with a family history across generations, and the name alone cannot establish a diagnosis.

translation: Or in a syndrome, as with “Wolcott”.
Follow that with “Rallison”, or hold your tongue.
16.sharh: The listener learns a difficult surname across the rhyme break. Wolcott–Rallison syndrome is a rare inherited condition in which very early diabetes can occur alongside skeletal and other disorders.

translation: There are many others, including singular rarities,
like the Madid among the metres of our poetry.
17.sharh: Madid is an Arabic metre rarely encountered in comparison with the more familiar ones. The doctor borrows a poet’s example to make room for uncommon diagnoses.

translation: They have all adopted certain traits.
When they befall a youngster, he thirsts and passes water.
18.sharh: Intense thirst and frequent urination are recognisable signs of high blood glucose. The brevity makes them memorable, although diabetes can also be present before either symptom is noticed.

translation: Hear my advice if it strikes and leaves you in doubt.
Is it the first or the second? Pay attention.
19.sharh: The learner moves from a list to a bedside. The difficult question is how to classify this particular person when familiar clues point in more than one direction.

translation: Skilled practitioners have told us here
of a hybrid type with no sure test of its own.
20.sharh: “Hybrid” conveys the difficulty of fitting a patient to one textbook picture. Insulin resistance can coexist with autoimmune diabetes, and this descriptive label does not establish a separate diagnosis.

translation: Its features overlapped until it claimed
to be both second and first together.
21.sharh: The disease itself gets to enter a double claim. Clinicians can bring the history and appropriate tests, including islet autoantibodies, to bear on features that overlap.

translation: The doctor was at a loss over the youngster.
Would treatment miss its mark or hit it?
22.sharh: The question now has consequences for the child in the room. The verb for success also suggests something striking its target, giving the doctor’s uncertainty a physical direction.

translation: He began to babble of the humours’ fictions,
staring hard at neck and armpits.
23.sharh: The obsolete language of bodily humours briefly takes over as the doctor flounders. Dark, velvety skin in neck or armpit folds can suggest insulin resistance, but cannot classify diabetes on its own.

translation: If wonder gets the better of you, my good man,
keep a close watch on that patient.
24.sharh: A brisk old Arabic address snaps the learner out of bewilderment. Close observation belongs to active clinical assessment, and a seriously ill child with suspected insulin deficiency needs urgent care.

translation: Soothe your soul if it starts finding fault.
The like of this has baffled great experts.
25.sharh: The anxious clinician becomes a person who needs care as well. Discovering that experts have shared this uncertainty can make it easier to reconsider a first impression.

translation: Then put your trust in our God, on whom all depend.
Seek His help and ask Him for support.
26.sharh: The invocation comes between looking closely at the patient and discussing treatment. It gives the clinician’s uncertainty a devotional expression within work that still needs doing.

translation: It may be right to meet those doubts
with insulin if the cause leaves you unsure.
27.sharh: When insulin deficiency is suspected, treatment may be needed before the precise diagnosis is settled, particularly in acute illness. This is a supervised clinical decision made for the patient’s condition.

translation: It has indeed helped the sick
by our Lord’s leave. Take heart.
28.sharh: He asks the clinician to draw courage from the patients insulin has already helped. That present-day confidence opens the way to a very different past.

translation: Before it, once the disease had set in,
only death released them from their illness.
29.sharh: The bleak line fits severe insulin deficiency in the years before replacement therapy. Untreated type 1 was fatal, while the course of other forms of diabetes could be quite different.

translation: Our almighty Lord willed that humanity
should see this grief lift. Here is what happened.
30.sharh: “Here is what happened” changes the pace of the lesson. A history of the first treatments will give an individual face to the suffering the poet has described.

translation: In a city beyond the farthest horizon,
whose people were fond of being first,
31.sharh: Toronto is introduced from the distant listener’s point of view. The city’s supposed love of coming first prepares a more precise claim about its place in medical history.

translation: against its cold they wrapped themselves in shawls
and face coverings, at home and on their travels.
32.sharh: Clothing gives a remote place a human scale. The established pairing of settling and travelling imagines the same cold following people wherever they go.

translation: They held it up to rival the world’s towns, Toronto,
its r given a u, as in the word rumtu.
33.sharh: He even teaches how to pronounce Toronto in his Arabic verse. Rumtu, “I sought”, supplies the vowel he wants on its r, giving the city’s name a tiny Arabic pronunciation lesson.

translation: In our last century, once it had seen
ten years, ten more and another two go by,
34.sharh: Counting the tens and the two years leads to 1922. The arithmetic slows the approach to the hospital bed until the date has settled in the listener’s mind.

translation: in a ward of one of its hospitals
a patient was laid up, suffering from dehydration,
35.sharh: The city narrows to a single ward at Toronto General Hospital. We meet the patient through a physical sign before we learn his name.

translation: a sick boy worn down by illness.
They call him Leonard Thompson.
36.sharh: The boy at last becomes an individual with a name. Thompson’s surviving hospital chart lets the reader follow the two January treatments behind the poem’s account.

translation: That is his name. It contains an undotted d,
normally still. I gave it a vowel for an easier flow.
37.sharh: The poet admits adjusting the foreign name to his metre. Arabic distinguishes d from its dotted neighbour dh, and a vowel after Leonard’s final d smooths the passage to Thompson.

translation: He fights death without a spear,
stretched out, his heart in turmoil.
38.sharh: The sickbed becomes the ground of an unequal contest. His outstretched body is almost motionless, while the heart within it is agitated.

translation: Diabetes had gone beyond all bounds,
so they declared war on it to drive it away.
39.sharh: The boy gains allies. The clinicians’ enemy is clearly the disease, which the poet has allowed to advance like an aggressor.

translation: Grief showed on his mother’s face.
She holds him while worry covers her.
40.sharh: The embrace lets the illness reach beyond the patient’s body into the life of his family. It belongs to the poet’s imagining of the bedside, while the clinical chart documents the boy’s condition and treatment.

translation: In his day the people of medicine
had brought the hormone out of its hiding place.
41.sharh: The earlier fight at the bedside depended on work away from it. The hormone is pictured as something brought out from concealment and made available to the sick.

translation: They extracted it from the organs of dogs
and of other animals, the wholesome and the fanged.
42.sharh: The poem ranges broadly across the animal world. Dogs figured in the Toronto experiments, and preparations from cattle pancreases were used in the early human treatment.

translation: They tried injecting the beasts,
and in their veins its command was obeyed.
43.sharh: The hormone is made a commander whose orders take effect out of sight. In the early animal experiments its effect could be measured as a fall in blood glucose.

translation: Then they resolved to give the boy an injection.
The turn of their insulin had come.
44.sharh: The boy and the extract, introduced separately, finally meet. At Toronto General the first trial injection was given on 11 January 1922.

translation: Wasting had left him worn threadbare.
After his injection he seemed to be well.
45.sharh: The contrast is compressed into a single injection. Thompson showed little benefit on 11 January. The striking improvement came on 23 January with a preparation purified by James Collip.

translation: He lived among them in good health for years.
Glory to Him by whose command he was made well.
46.sharh: Thompson lived another thirteen years with insulin. “In good health” expresses the gift of those years and should be read in light of his continued dependence on treatment.

translation: They took pride in being first. Well they might.
Glory to Him who crowned them with that achievement.
47.sharh: The doctors are allowed their pride in an achievement earned through work. A crown then enters the picture, and in the poet’s devotional telling it is God who gives it.

translation: They commemorated it on their currency,
on a hundred-dollar note of high value,
48.sharh: The discovery leaves the archives for an object people handle in daily life. A Canadian hundred-dollar note issued in 2011 carries the image that the next couplet describes.

translation: with a drawing of a vial for this antidote,
slender at the waist, covered and gleaming.
49.sharh: The poet gives the shining, stoppered bottle a waist. The Bank of Canada identifies the model on the note as an early insulin bottle dating to 1923.

translation: In our time insulin has had children.
It fathered a fast one, “Ra”, among its offspring,
50.sharh: Insulin becomes a parent. The poet calls its fast child “Ra”, borrowing the start of the English word rapid as a nickname that will fit the rhyme.

translation: and fathered a slow one, “Lo”. When it travels
it seems sluggish with sleep.
51.sharh: “Lo” comes from long in long-acting insulin. The drowsy child’s gait makes a memorable contrast with rapid action, while the medical distinction concerns how long and how quickly a preparation works.

translation: Its forms have grown diverse for us.
Its deeds have borne out its words.
52.sharh: Once insulin has a family, it can make promises too. Its different preparations bear out their descriptions through their different patterns of action.

translation: Today they have reproduced it in the laboratory
as though it were extracted from a human being.
53.sharh: Recombinant human insulin has the same amino-acid sequence as the body’s own insulin. Other manufactured forms are analogues deliberately altered to change how they act.

translation: Praise be to God for His blessings,
and thanks be to God for His generosity.
54.sharh: The refrain of thanks marks the close of the history. It also gives the speaker a pause before he turns to the people who must live with the choices these discoveries have made possible.

translation: Before we draw our words to a close,
let us bring something to people’s attention.
55.sharh: The addressee changes. A passage once directed to the puzzled clinician now makes room for patients, relatives and anyone seeking an answer about health.

translation: Do not take your medicine from the nets.
The spider is master of snares.
56.sharh: A web for exchanging information becomes a spider’s trap. The image warns against relying on unverified online treatment claims. Reliable medical services also publish guidance online.

translation: In our time science has driven the practice of medicine
and urged it towards sound judgement.
57.sharh: The verb for driving evokes someone urging a caravan on. Medicine can improve its aim by testing a claim and revising it in the light of what happens.

translation: Not everything I have mentioned here
suits everyone or is within our reach.
58.sharh: Suitability and access are two separate questions. A treatment described in a poem may be inappropriate for a particular person or unavailable where that person lives.

translation: Ask a skilled and attentive doctor
about injections, a pump or a tablet.
59.sharh: A pump is a way of delivering insulin, while tablets have different uses. For type 1, the need for insulin remains whichever delivery method the patient and team choose.

translation: And not every injection is insulin.
If you are unsure, ask until you understand.
60.sharh: A pen or syringe tells the patient how a medicine enters the body, not what the medicine is. There are injectable medicines for type 2 diabetes which do not replace insulin in type 1.

translation: Diet is the chief remedy, as you see.
Our forebears said so, as the saying goes.
61.sharh: The claim about diet is explicitly passed down as a maxim. Food choices matter across diabetes care, but diet cannot replace insulin in type 1 and may need to be combined with medication in type 2.

translation: With a balanced diet the patient’s condition
comes into order, provided he gets up and walks.
62.sharh: Walking gives the maxim a modest daily action. Nutrition and activity can help manage blood glucose, with plans adapted to the individual and to the effects of treatment.

translation: Remember to keep an eye on other ailments,
whether they come alongside or follow as things go awry.
63.sharh: Some conditions coexist with diabetes, while others can develop as complications. The studio gloss gives thyroid disease and protein in the urine as examples, which call for different kinds of follow-up.

translation: A team has drawn up this treatment,
with the patient and companion at its head.
64.sharh: For a child, much of daily care takes place with family far from the clinic. Placing the patient and companion at the head of the team recognises the knowledge and work that happen there.

translation: We ask God to grant healing to humankind
and to extend it to us and all who give thanks.
65.sharh: The prayer opens out from one patient’s history to humanity. The physician includes himself again, returning to the “us” that appeared near the beginning.

translation: Perhaps something has come into sight on the horizon
that sends joy deep within.
66.sharh: The contrast is between a far horizon and an emotion felt deep within. The poem voices a hope about future treatment without identifying a particular discovery or promising a cure.

translation: Trustworthy authorities tell us that on diabetes
whole volumes have already been written.
67.sharh: A lesson short enough to recite is set beside shelves of medical writing. That comparison prepares the speaker to say exactly how much he thinks he has offered.

translation: The little I have mentioned here
is a mere trickle from an abundant flood.
68.sharh: Ghayd and fayd, a dwindling quantity and an overflow, differ by a single consonant. A tiny change in sound measures the distance between this poem and the literature behind it.

translation: Praise be to God for what He made easy,
and thanks as long as night travels on or draws back.
69.sharh: After the specific dates and names, gratitude takes its rhythm from the passing night. It answers the cloud rising through the sky near the beginning.

translation: I close with blessings and peace
upon the Prophet, foremost of humankind.
70.sharh: The blessing that opened the lesson closes it. The final word for humankind also recalls the people he turned to address once the medical history was told.

4.1.2.head: أُرجوزَة
4.1.2.meaning: Urjuza is a poem in rajaz metre, often used to put a subject into memorable verse.

5.2.4.head: فاعَ
5.2.4.meaning: To rise and spread, as a scent fills the air.

7.2.4.head: أَجمَلَ
7.2.4.meaning: To give the main divisions in summary.

9.2.3.head: صَمّاء
9.2.3.meaning: Endocrine, describing secretion into the bloodstream. Here the poet means the hormone-producing tissue of the pancreas.

10.1.3.head: اِنكَمى
10.1.3.meaning: To conceal oneself or lie hidden.

10.2.5.head: لادا
10.2.5.meaning: LADA stands for latent autoimmune diabetes in adults.

11.2.6.head: زِمام
11.2.6.meaning: A rein or halter by which an animal is led.

12.1.4.head: حُبلى
12.1.4.meaning: Pregnant. The Arabic word sounds like the cord cut in the next half.

12.2.4.head: حَبل
12.2.4.meaning: The umbilical cord, with the last vowel drawn out for the rhyme.

13.1.4-5.head: ما أَلا
13.1.4-5.meaning: “It did not slacken.” The illness may persist after pregnancy.

13.2.6.head: قَلى
13.2.6.meaning: To forsake or turn away from someone.

15.1.3.head: ضَرب
15.1.3.meaning: Giving an example to illustrate a point.

15.2.5.head: مودي
15.2.5.meaning: MODY stands for maturity-onset diabetes of the young, a group of single-gene forms of diabetes.

16.1.5.head: وُلكُت
16.1.5.meaning: Wolcott, the first surname in Wolcott–Rallison syndrome.

16.2.3.head: رالِسُن
16.2.3.meaning: Rallison completes the name of the rare inherited syndrome associated with very early diabetes.

17.2.4.head: مَديد
17.2.4.meaning: Madid is an Arabic verse metre. Its name also suggests length or extension.

18.2.4.head: ظَمِئَ
18.2.4.meaning: To be thirsty. The poet lightens the final consonant of the usual Arabic verb.

20.1.5.head: حاذِق
20.1.5.meaning: Skilled or proficient, here an experienced practitioner.

20.2.2.head: هَجين
20.2.2.meaning: Mixed in its features. Here the word describes a clinical puzzle about diabetes type.

20.2.5.head: مِصداق
20.2.5.meaning: Evidence that would bear out a claim.

23.1.4-5.head: فِرى الأَخلاط
23.1.4-5.meaning: “Fictions of the humours.” Humoral medicine explained disease through supposed imbalances of bodily fluids.

23.2.2-3.head: الجيد وَالآباط
23.2.2-3.meaning: Neck and armpits, skin folds where a clinician might look for the dark, velvety changes of acanthosis nigricans.

24.1.3-5.head: لا أَبا لَكَ
24.1.3-5.meaning: “May you have no father.” An old emphatic address used here to urge attention.

26.1.5.head: الصَّمَد
26.1.5.meaning: Al-Samad, a Qur’anic name of God, the One to whom all turn in need.

27.2.1.head: إِنسُلين
27.2.1.meaning: Insulin is a pancreatic hormone also used as a medicine to manage blood glucose.

28.1.4.head: سَقيم
28.1.4.meaning: An ill person. The plural here means the people helped by treatment.

29.2.2.head: فَدى
29.2.2.meaning: To ransom or release someone from a predicament.

30.2.2.head: اِنجَلى
30.2.2.meaning: To lift or clear, as grief does here. The usual final vowel after an falls away in the recitation.

32.1.3.head: تَلَفَّعَ
32.1.3.meaning: To wrap oneself up in a garment.

32.2.1.head: لِثام
32.2.1.meaning: A covering drawn across the lower face.

32.2.3-4.head: الحِلّ وَالتِّرحال
32.2.3-4.meaning: “Settling and travelling”, an established pairing for being at home or away.

33.1.5.head: تورُنتو
33.1.5.meaning: Toronto, the Canadian city where Thompson received the early pancreatic extracts in 1922.

33.2.5.head: رامَ
33.2.5.meaning: To seek or intend. Its first-person form gives the vowel the poet wants for Toronto.

36.1.4.head: مُثخَن
36.1.4.meaning: Severely weakened, as if weighed down by illness.

36.2.2-3.head: لِنَرد ثُمسَن
36.2.2-3.meaning: Leonard Thompson, the boy treated at Toronto General Hospital in January 1922. The Arabic gives the poet’s metrical form of the name.

37.1.4-5.head: دال مُهمَلَة
37.1.4-5.meaning: An undotted dal, the Arabic letter for d as distinct from its dotted counterpart for dh.

39.2.1.head: ناصَبَ
39.2.1.meaning: To confront someone openly as an adversary.

41.2.5.head: كِنان
41.2.5.meaning: A cover or shelter concealing something within.

42.1.3.head: حَشى
42.1.3.meaning: The inward organs. In the history of insulin, the organ meant is the pancreas.

44.1.1.head: أَزمَعَ
44.1.1.meaning: To decide on a course of action.

45.1.5.head: مُهتَرِئ
45.1.5.meaning: Worn out or frayed like old fabric.

49.1.4.head: تِرياق
49.1.4.meaning: Tiryaq is an antidote, used figuratively here for insulin.

49.2.1.head: مُخَصَّر
49.2.1.meaning: Narrow at the middle, as if it had a waist.

50.2.3.head: را
50.2.3.meaning: “Ra” is the poet’s nickname for rapid-acting insulin, from the English word rapid.

51.1.3.head: لو
51.1.3.meaning: “Lo” stands for the beginning of long in long-acting insulin.

56.2.3.head: شِراك
56.2.3.meaning: Snares or traps, answering the nets or web of the first half.

57.1.3.head: حَدا
57.1.3.meaning: To drive a caravan onward, here to guide the progress of medicine.

59.2.3.head: مَضَخَّة
59.2.3.meaning: A pump that delivers insulin according to a treatment plan.

61.1.3.head: حِميَة
61.1.3.meaning: A dietary regimen. The poet introduces the saying as an inherited maxim.

64.2.3.head: رَفيق
64.2.3.meaning: A companion or caregiver, including the family of a child with diabetes.

68.1.6.head: غَيض
68.1.6.meaning: A dwindling of water, hence a small quantity.
